clue.text: One Gentleman of Verona, please, out of costume

indicators.note: stripped of its outfit, the string loses its outer letters

parts.note: an Italian gentleman is a signor
to please is to amuse

explanation.surface: A character from Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona begs to be let out of his stage costume.
explanation.walkthrough: This puzzle ran on April Fool's Day, and every 'one' in it is a fool. The Shakespeare play is a red herring: Verona just makes the gentleman Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant person, one of the puzzle's many kinds of fool.

clue.text: One Direction, thrice perhaps on tour

indicators.note: letters that go touring end up moved around

parts.note: three directions: WAY, S (south) and NE (north-east)

explanation.surface: The boy band One Direction heads off on a world tour, perhaps for the third time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One Direction' reads as the band's name, but the clue splits there: 'One' is the definition and 'Direction' starts the wordplay. 'Perhaps' warns that any three directions will do.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawney is an old, originally Scottish word for a simpleton.

clue.text: Wound up, Porky packs fine punch

indicators.note: Porky packs the letter inside itself
wound back up, the letters run the other way (in a down clue, bottom to top)

parts.note: porky pie is rhyming slang for a lie, so a porky is a fib
F is the pencil abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A wound-up character called Porky throws a good punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porky' looks like a name or a pig; it is British rhyming slang (pork pie = lie). F goes in after FIB's first letter, then the lot is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain informal synonym: to biff someone is to hit them with your fist.

clue.text: Record: outliers in indexing are all ground-based

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: the letters lying outermost in each word

parts.note: outer letters
outer letters
outer letters

explanation.surface: A record-keeper notes that, apart from a few outliers, everything in the index sits on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outliers' is taken literally: the letters lying outside, at each end of the three words that follow. EPIGAEAL is a biologist's word for living on the surface of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Epigaeal describes organisms living or growing on the ground's surface.

clue.text: One each covered by lead bucket?

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
ea. is the abbreviation for each
to bucket down is to rain hard

explanation.surface: Every item gets a lead bucket as its lid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucket' looks like a noun but works as the verb, as in 'it's bucketing down'.
explanation.definitionFit: A peabrain is someone with a brain the size of a pea: a fool.

clue.text: Aussie one, not half sweet, embracing Georgia

indicators.note: only half the word is kept

parts.note: a bonbon is a sweet; take half of it
GA is the US postal abbreviation for Georgia

explanation.surface: An Australian with only half a sweet tooth gives Georgia a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is often British slang for 'very much'; here it is literal, halving BONBON.
explanation.definitionFit: Bogan is Australian slang for an uncouth, unsophisticated person.

clue.text: There's no better one

definitions.meaning: the best ever, in a modern sporting acronym
one of the puzzle's fools: an animal name for a silly person

explanation.surface: Someone is praised as the very best there is.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a single boast, but it splits in two: GOAT is Greatest Of All Time, and to act the goat is to play the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: The GOAT has no better; and a silly old goat is a fool.

clue.text: One son, little monkey, spoilt the surprise

parts.note: s. is the abbreviation for son
a mischievous child is a little monkey, or an imp
LET ON: revealed the secret

explanation.surface: A parent grumbles that their mischievous son gave away the surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little monkey' is an affectionate name for a naughty child, which is also what an imp is.
explanation.definitionFit: A simpleton is a foolish, gullible person.

clue.text: One Down: anagram's hiding

indicators.note: the words keep the answer hidden inside them

parts.note: the last letter of Down and the first three of anagram

explanation.surface: A clue announces that its one down answer is concealed in an anagram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anagram' is bait: there is no anagram, just a word hidden across 'Down' and 'anagram'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nana is British slang for a silly person, as in 'you big nana'.

clue.text: One tick working a little lower

parts.note: a tick and a mo are both a moment
a machine that is working is on
a young cow: a little animal that lows

explanation.surface: A flea-like tick, busy at work, crawls a little further down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' is not 'further down' but 'one who lows', i.e. moos; a little one of those is a calf.
explanation.definitionFit: A mooncalf is a foolish, absent-minded person.

clue.text: Irish one heading back with a dog after biting bishop

indicators.note: the whole string sets off the way it came

parts.note: w. is the abbreviation for with
as printed
as printed
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: An Irishman walks home with his dog, which has just bitten a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: Build W + A + D(B)OG first, then turn all of it around.
explanation.definitionFit: Gobdaw is Irish slang for a fool or a gullible person.

clue.text: Unspecified number given a quarter turn, whichever one

definitions.note: in this puzzle's theme, one means a fool

indicators.note: rotated through ninety degrees, so the letter for an unspecified number is turned on its side and becomes a different capital

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number in maths, as in to the nth degree
any means whichever, as in take any you like

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter's instruction: rotate a variable, then pick any one you like.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotate a capital N by a right angle and it looks like a Z. Every 'one' in this puzzle means a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A zany was a clown's comic sidekick in old Italian comedy, so a buffoon.

clue.text: Ordering refreshments in court?

definitions.meaning: where you order drinks in a pub
a prisoner stands at the rail facing the judge

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you can order drinks during a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: The pub bar and the bar of a courtroom share the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: You order at the bar of a pub; a prisoner stands at the bar of the court.

clue.text: Thanks to Havertz, red card

parts.note: ta is British informal thanks
rot is German for red; Kai Havertz is a German footballer

explanation.surface: A referee's red card is thanks to Havertz's foul.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface makes 'red card' look like one unit; 'to Havertz' means 'in German', splitting off 'card' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarot is one of the cards of a fortune-telling pack.

clue.text: Trump's one calumny upset NBC, heading off the stars

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a down clue runs it bottom to top
the first letter is taken off

parts.note: slinging mud is calumny
N removed
your stars decide your luck

explanation.surface: Donald Trump, riled by a slanderous story on NBC, storms off to the stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump's one' means an American's word for a fool, the kind Trump might use.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumb cluck is American slang for a stupid person.

clue.text: Not entirely happy about one

indicators.note: the word is not given in full: its last letter goes
turned about, it runs backwards

parts.note: happy = drunk, tipsy; lose the K

explanation.surface: Someone is not altogether pleased about a certain person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy' here is the British sense of slightly drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurd is a variant spelling of nerd, a socially awkward or foolish person.

clue.text: One indicates detective employed by Spooner?

definitions.note: in this puzzle's theme, one means a fool

indicators.note: said the way Reverend Spooner would, swapping the opening sounds of the two words

parts.note: to tip is to indicate or hint, as in tipping someone off
a dick is slang for a detective, as in private dick; said aloud it is dik

explanation.surface: A detective story in which a clue points to the culprit.
explanation.walkthrough: TIPS DICK with its opening sounds exchanged becomes DIPS TICK. Every 'one' in this puzzle means a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipstick is informal slang for a stupid person, an idiot.

clue.text: This time alpha particle appears at intervals

parts.note: alpha is the phonetic-alphabet name for A

indicators.note: only every other letter shows

parts.note: P-a-R-t-I-c-L-e: odd letters

explanation.surface: A physicist says that at this moment an alpha particle keeps flickering into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This time' is the month the puzzle appeared: it ran on 1 April, which is why every 'one' is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle was published in April, so April is 'this time'.

clue.text: A gross baby, born today in a field?

definitions.note: Agrarian is an adjective meaning 'of the land'; 'in a field' is a whimsical stand-in.

parts.note: as printed
gr. is the abbreviation for gross
someone born on 1 April has the star sign Aries: an Arian

explanation.surface: A mucky newborn baby arrives today, out in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Today' is the puzzle's date, 1 April, which falls under Aries; an Arian is someone born under that sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Agrarian means relating to fields and farming.

clue.text: Cut Pointless — 21s haven't got it

definitions.note: 21 is FOOL, so this says fools lack it; the definition is a noun phrase for the quality they lack

indicators.note: cut short, so the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: something pointless is of no use

explanation.surface: A TV quiz show called Pointless is axed, with a jibe at the contestants.
explanation.walkthrough: Pointless is a BBC quiz show, but here it means 'no use'. 21 Down is FOOL, so 21s are fools.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is British informal for common sense or practical intelligence, which a fool lacks.

clue.text: It perhaps rather fuzzily aired Bugs Bunny features?

indicators.note: said out loud, and not too carefully

parts.note: Bugs Bunny's famous buck teeth: a pair of teeth, slurred

explanation.surface: A cartoon fan asks whether Bugs Bunny's features were broadcast a bit blurrily.
explanation.walkthrough: It is Italian vermouth, as in gin and It, which is drunk before a meal. The sound is only approximate, hence 'rather fuzzily'.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian vermouth is an example of an aperitif, a drink taken before eating.

clue.text: 18A is what one's after: dessert

definitions.meaning: 18A is APRIL; the word that follows it on 1 April names what every 'one' here is
a pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream

explanation.surface: In April, someone is looking forward to their pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream. 'One' across this puzzle has meant a fool, and FOOL follows APRIL.
explanation.definitionFit: April Fool comes after April; a fool is also a fruit dessert.

clue.text: Contents of incendiary bomb repulsed vegan musician

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words
pushed back, it runs the other way

parts.note: incendiar(Y BOM)b

explanation.surface: A vegan musician recoils at what is packed inside a firebomb.
explanation.walkthrough: Moby is an American electronic musician known for his veganism.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the American electronic artist is well known for his animal-rights campaigning.

clue.text: One indulged after mass finished

parts.note: m is the symbol for mass
time's up: finished
to pet is to pamper or indulge

explanation.surface: Someone treats themself once church is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass finished' paints a church service, but mass is the physics symbol M.
explanation.definitionFit: Muppet is British slang for a fool.

clue.text: Puzzle about buffoons on and off, sadly not caught

parts.note: re means about, concerning, as in a letter heading

indicators.note: in cricket a catch not taken is dropped, so these letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: the letters of on and off together, in a sorry jumbled state; the joining and supplies no letters

explanation.surface: A puzzle about clowns who keep falling over, sadly failing to catch each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' jumbles the letters of ON and OFF into FFOON, which 'not caught' (a dropped catch, in cricket) removes from BUFFOONS to leave BUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a word puzzle in which pictures or symbols stand for words or syllables.

clue.text: One leap across South River

parts.note: a jeté is a ballet leap
S is south
R is river

explanation.surface: Someone jumps across a river in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: The jeté is a ballet jump, from French for 'thrown'.
explanation.definitionFit: A jester is a professional fool at court.

clue.text: One, after change of heart, reserved parrot

definitions.note: in this puzzle's theme, one means a fool

indicators.note: a change of heart is a turnaround, so the letters of the word for reserved are changed round

parts.note: a cold manner is reserved and distant
Poll, or Polly, is a traditional name for a parrot

explanation.surface: Someone who was once standoffish has warmed up, like a pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change of heart' turns COLD into CLOD by swapping its middle letters. Every 'one' in this puzzle means a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Clodpoll is an archaic word for a blockhead or dimwit, literally a clod-head.

clue.text: Clown prince repeatedly evading police officer

indicators.note: escaping from, so these letters are removed from the officers

parts.note: a cop is a police officer, here taken twice because the escape is repeated
P is the standard abbreviation for prince, given twice

explanation.surface: A royal keeps slipping past the constable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' doubles the whole step: P slips out of COP once, and again, leaving CO twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Coco the Clown was a famous circus performer in Britain, the stage name of Nikolai Poliakoff.

clue.text: Impressed by the writer, can much upset one?

definitions.note: in this puzzle's theme, one means a fool

indicators.note: pressed into something, so the rearranged letters are pressed inside

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter, who is me

indicators.note: knocked over and disordered, so the letters of can much are rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter asks whether something can bother them so much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges CAN MUCH into UMCHANC, and 'Impressed by' puts it inside ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A mumchance is an archaic word for a silent, tongue-tied simpleton.

clue.text: Person hired nice car

explanation.surface: Someone rents a smart car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as hiring a car; in fact 'hired' belongs with 'Person'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two clipped words: mercenary, a soldier paid to fight, and Mercedes, the German luxury make.
